newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch outline plans to tackle traffic gridlock.
newsitem.headline: Dutch outline plans to tackle traffic gridlock.

text.p: The Netherlands, at the heart of Europe's busy trading routes, plans to spend an extra $1.25 billion fighting road congestion, Transport Minister Annemarie Jorritsma says.

The Dutch propose building new road links and extra lanes in specific traffic corridors to ease the flow of goods and people in and around major urban centres and along key trade routes to Germany and Belgium.
She told an American Chamber of Commerce lunch in The Hague that she hoped to tackle severe traffic problems under a new Dutch transport plan.
"Many parts of our road networks have already reached the limits of their capacity. Building more roads is not a realistic option," she said.
"It is essential for our economic growth that our transport infrastructure keeps pace with the increasing volume of traffic in and through our small country," Jorritsma said.
"The new integrated transport plan for The Netherlands, tabled in parliament a month ago, will require an additional investment of one billion Ecus."
Big new trans-shipment terminals were also under consideration, though Jorritsma did not detail these.

The Dutch will also invest in improving the efficiency of the existing road network, introducing special lanes which can be reversed during peak-hours, ramp metering, freight-only lanes and speed limits linked to specific time periods.
Priority will also be given to "economically important traffic" -- deliveries of goods to shops and small businesses -- by introducing special traffic lanes in urban areas.
Public transport will also be boosted to discourage private car use.
The Dutch have spent heavily on a new high-speed rail link to Brussels and several light rail lines are projected.
Road-pricing (tolls) will be introduced on certain main links in 2000-2001.

Under a "driver pays" policy, Jorritsma said she favoured raising variable costs -- from July 1997 excise duty on petrol will go up by 11 guilder cents per litre and on diesel by five cents -- and reducing fixed costs for motorists.

Rail, short sea-shipping and inland waterway traffic will also be developed, including the Betuwe freight-only rail link between Rotterdam and the industrial heartlands of Germany, the Netherlands' biggest trading partner, due to be completed in 2005.
Jorritsma also touched on the explosive growth in telecoms in The Netherlands which, she said, would make the country an "information mainport" in Europe.
The Dutch have dismantled barriers to telecoms competition, awarding mobile network licences. "I'm working to abolish the last remaining monopolies in telecoms by July 1998," she said.
Jorritsma said The Netherlands was particularly attractive to telecoms firms because of its low tariffs for business users, increased competition and accessibility.
Only the United States and Denmark have more (telephone) connections per capita, she said.
The information sector was founded on a strong publishing and audio-visual industry, a high level of education, top-level knowledge centres and the strong telecoms sector, she added.
"Our advanced information society...is contributing to an upswing in the economic climate in our country," Jorritsma said.
